extracted.intended_audience: architects, art historians, critics, and educated readers of architectural criticism
extracted.subtask_description: Critical evaluation of Venetian architecture and its historical styles, tracing formation, influences, and decline; explains how to judge quality in buildings and monuments. Targets assessment of form, material truth, symbolism, ornament, and the maker's moral/intellectual character.

rubrics_metrics.name: Architectural_feature_recognition
rubrics_metrics.description: The reader should be able to recognise the basic structural elements (nave, aisles, clerestory, vaulting shaft, grouped shafts, etc.) and understand their spatial relationships.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples given: a basilica with a nave much higher than aisles, nave separated by rows of shafts supporting clerestory walls and a gabled wooden roof; grouped and added vaulting shafts originate in wooden construction. Knowing these parts enables identification of style and period.

rubrics_metrics.name: Material_evolution_and_structural_truth
rubrics_metrics.description: Good architecture respects and expresses the truth of its materials and structural origins (e.g., stone forms retaining the shapes required by earlier wooden constructions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ruskin describes how Northern wooden uprights became petrified in stone as vaulting shafts; the 'petrified' form that honestly records its wooden origins is a positive quality. Conversely, disguising structural truth is implied as criticism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinctive_stylistic_character
rubrics_metrics.description: Each school/style should manifest its characteristic formal vocabulary (e.g., 'rough but majestic' Northern work: round-arched, grouped shafts, added vaulting shafts, active imagery).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use features (arches, shafts, imagery, mouldings) to ascribe work to Lombard, Byzantine, Arab, Gothic, etc. The author enumerates features as identifying marks for Northern/Lombard and Venetian schools.

rubrics_metrics.name: Influence_and_refinement_by_cultural_contact
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess how external cultural influences (e.g., Arab) refine, spiritualise, or corrupt native architectural forms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ruskin argues Arab influence refined Northern work into Gothic forms (Pisan-Komanesque, Tuscan Giottesque, Veronese Gothic). Evaluate whether such influences elevate or degrade the native style.

rubrics_metrics.name: Historical_and_chronological_fidelity
rubrics_metrics.description: Dating and tracing the succession of styles is necessary for evaluation; certain central dates fix stylistic phases (e.g., 1180 as central for a transitional Venetian Arabic style).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use masonry, sculpture, costume in figures, and changes in material/stone size to determine periods (examples: differences in capitals and stone from 14th vs 15th century on the Ducal Palace). Accurate chronology supports judgments of originality and decline.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriateness_of_adaptation
rubrics_metrics.description: Adopted details from other cultures must be appropriate to function and context (e.g., Venetians imitated Arabian domestic details but avoided mosque forms in churches).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge substitutions: are foreign details harmoniously adapted (positive) or inappropriately applied to incompatible building types (negative)?

rubrics_metrics.name: Truth_and_vitality
rubrics_metrics.description: Architecture must possess 'truth and vitality'; loss of these signals corruption and decline.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ruskin cites a general 'loss of truth and vitality' across architectures of his time as the first sign of change/decline. Compare earlier living expression (fourteenth-century virtues) with later lifeless or affected treatment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoidance_of_excessive_or_meaningless_ornament
rubrics_metrics.description: Ornament must be meaningful and subordinate to truth; excessive, meaningless ornamentation denotes corruption.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Corrupted Gothics 'lost themselves in every species of extravagance' and Italian work effloresced into 'meaningless ornamentation' (examples: Certosa of Pavia, Cathedral of Como, Porta della Carta). Ornament that obscures form or truth is blamed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maker's_moral_and_intellectual_character_as_evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: The character and honesty of the workmen (sculptors, architects) is evidential for the quality of the work; dishonesty or moral corruption in makers indicates inferiority of the architecture.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ruskin uses particular facts (e.g., the sculptor of the Vendramin tomb was banished for forgery) as testimony. Such biographical or documentary proofs are part of judging authenticity and value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Honesty_in_representation
rubrics_metrics.description: Representational works (tombs, statues) should be truthful, not deceitfully tailored to viewpoint; partial or dishonest finishing to cheat the spectator is a fault.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: the Vendramin effigy was finished only on the side expected to be seen, producing 'half a face' and a 'monstrous mask'; Ruskin condemns this as dishonest and morally cold workmanship.

rubrics_metrics.name: Originality_vs_mechanical_copying
rubrics_metrics.description: A work should show invention rather than clumsy copying of earlier forms; slavish imitation impoverishes meaning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fifteenth-century workmen simply copied earlier capitals; the copied virtues lost living expression and spiritual elements (e.g., the hand of God disappears). Mechanical copying is criticized as lacking wit and depth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Retention_of_symbolic_and_spiritual_meaning
rubrics_metrics.description: Symbols and spiritual meanings originally present in design should be preserved; their removal or inversion indicates spiritual and aesthetic impoverishment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ruskin contrasts the fourteenth-century 'Hope' with a visible hand of God and explicit iconography to the later version where 'the hand of God is gone' and Hope appears to 'pray to the sun'—a loss of theological/symbolic integrity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Universality_of_aesthetic_principle
rubrics_metrics.description: There exists a universal law of right by which good architecture can be distinguished from bad, independent of style or national feeling.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ruskin asserts that good design may be indisputably discerned and applied to Gothic, Greek, Arab works alike; judgments should rest on principle (truth, wisdom, nobility) rather than mere opinion or partisanship.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use_of_two_kinds_of_evidence_in_criticism
rubrics_metrics.description: Criticism should rely on (1) particular incidents/facts about makers (testimony) and (2) the critic's cultivated sense of systematic ugliness or beauty intrinsic to the architecture.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ruskin says he will use documentary/factual testimony (forgery, dishonest cutting) and the reader's awakened sense of a 'systematic ugliness' to argue inferiority of later work; both empirical and sensorial evidence are valid.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proportion_and_elegance_of_profile
rubrics_metrics.description: Correct elegance of profiles and proportions, and refined ornamentation and detailing, are marks of excellence in sculptural/architectural work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quoted praise of the Vendramin tomb (Selvatico) emphasizes 'corretta eleganza di profili e di proporzioni' and 'squisitezza d'ornamenti' as virtues—though Ruskin notes such formal qualities may coexist with other failures (e.g., lack of true portrait likeness).
